Messages.Body:
V:EKN Tournament Rules -
4.4. Card Elevation and Disposition
Players must keep their cards above the level of the playing surface.
Revealing cards in your hand or uncontrolled area to an opponent is not
allowed.

OK, I must be missing something here because I really fail to see how
being prevented from showing your cards to other players is of any
benefit to the game whatsoever.

The big advantage of being able to show a card to other players is that
it provides a quick, clear, unambiguous message, i.e., 'I have such and
such a card'. As the saying goes, a picture is worth a thousand words.

Particularly in VTES where the metagame revolves around deception and
subterfuge, a concrete sighting of a card is often the only way to
convince a player that you do in fact have a certain card.

The way I see it, being prevented from showing cards to other players
does absolutely nothing to improve the game, and degrades the quality
of play by creating unneccesary confusion and ambiguity (in a situation
where opposite is desired, of course!).

Just my two cents,

Justicar.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Justicar <just...@my-deja.com> writes:

>V:EKN Tournament Rules -
>4.4. Card Elevation and Disposition
>Players must keep their cards above the level of the playing surface.
>Revealing cards in your hand or uncontrolled area to an opponent is not
>allowed.
>
>OK, I must be missing something here because I really fail to see how
>being prevented from showing your cards to other players is of any
>benefit to the game whatsoever.

Simple: it keeps players from cooperating too closely. That's the
interesting trade-off in multiplayer games: you can cooperate to mutual
advantage, but to do so you often must risk more than you might normally
lose if you hadn't cooperated. Preventing players from revealing cards
facilitates this dynamic: players can cooperate heavily in the play of
their cards, but to do so they must trust that their ally has the card(s)
he claims to have and that he's not just leading them on.

It also penalizes that sort of cooperation by forcing players to reveal
to the entire table what they would prefer to remain hidden. In short,
you can cooperate in card play but you lose the element of surprise in
doing so.

>Particularly in VTES where the metagame revolves around deception and
>subterfuge, a concrete sighting of a card is often the only way to
>convince a player that you do in fact have a certain card.

Correct. And this is bad. Cooperation which is too easy and too effective
penalizes players who built better decks, outguessed the metagame, and
have played more effectively on their own. Same reason that the preditor-
prey relationship is used in the game.

>The way I see it, being prevented from showing cards to other players
>does absolutely nothing to improve the game, and degrades the quality
>of play by creating unneccesary confusion and ambiguity (in a situation
>where opposite is desired, of course!).

It depends on what you mean. The "confusion and ambiguity" you're talking
about is just how information is handled. The victim of such conspiracies
obviously desires the confusion and ambiguity - not the opposite. So it
depends on who you talk to.

It's a matter of judgement to what extent conspiracies and gang-ups are
a "good thing" in this game and should be facilitated by the rules. What
you're missing is that the designer's judgement about it is obviously
different than yours.

Fred

>Particularly in VTES where the metagame revolves around deception and
>subterfuge, a concrete sighting of a card is often the only way to
>convince a player that you do in fact have a certain card.

Being unable to PROVE that you do in fact have a certain card
-maintains- the deception and subterfuge, providing a certain
"Paranoia"-like feel to the game. (The Computer is your Friend). It
wouldn't be as good of a game if people were nice to each other. It
also helps maintain the "being out for yourself first" aspect of the
game, which is required for the game to function properly. If one
player is not attempting to win, the table frequently becomes
unbalanced.

If you can show your cards to other players, you decrease the strategy
involved in the game. It goes from something-akin-to-chess, with its
possible moves and countermoves and twists and turns, to
something-akin-to-checkers, which was solved long ago and now is
merely a case of "If A, do B". If you show a Skin of Steel to your
predator, he probably doesn't waste his last rush on you and instead
rushes backwards. If you can only *say* "I have a Skin of Steel.
Don't waste your time", then he might, despite your smiling honest
face and outwardly pure appearance, decide you're full of it and try
going forwards anyway. This uncertainty is vital to the game.

>The way I see it, being prevented from showing cards to other players
>does absolutely nothing to improve the game, and degrades the quality
>of play by creating unneccesary confusion and ambiguity (in a situation
>where opposite is desired, of course!).

Not so. There is no confusion and ambiguity about what you have in
your own hand, which is what you're supposed to be primarily focused
on. There might be plenty of confusion regarding what's in OTHER
players' hands... which is to be expected when dealing with four other
shady, nefarious Methuselahs who are totally out for themselves and
who MIGHT provide accurate information but not necessarily so.

-- Derek

You'll just have to work on your persuasion skills, eh? I have
difficulty coming up with a situation where I'd -want- to show an
erratic player (or even a non-erratic player) one of my cards. Say
he's rushing cross-table and I say "I have a Skin of Steel. Don't
waste your time." If he believes me, that's good! If he doesn't,
well, I -do- have the Skin of Steel and his rush will go nowhere.
Sure, maybe I wanted to use it against my prey when he blocked one of
my bleeds, but that's life when you have an erratic player on the
table. Not all events are predictable.

I think if I -really- wanted to save my SoS, I'd spend my time
explaining why rushing me cross-table didn't help him win the game.
If rushing me DOES help him win the game, then he's not acting
erratically, is he?

>But this just penalises new players or players who don't play very

The personalities of the PLAYERS should not be at issue regarding whom
to trust. The whole issue of trust/no trust should be totally
dependent on the game situation. Hence, a new player or player who
doesn't play very often should be able to look at the table and say
"OK, *this* person is claiming to want to help, but he's mostly just
going to be out for himself, whereas *this* person actually has a
reason to want me to be helped, therefore...", and it shouldn't matter
if they know the real-life people or not. I've been able to pull off
successful deals in tournaments with people I've never seen before.

>encourages alliances between people who know each other pre-game
>because of the increased risk involved in not being able to verify your
>ally's intentions.

Which will get both players booted under the collusion rule. This is
a four or five-player game. More specifically, it is a 1 vs 1 vs 1 vs
1 (vs 1)-player game. Two players making a pre-game "alliance" should
NEVER happen, as the seating order or table dynamics could make such
an alliance not in one player's best interests. Two players looking
at the first two turns and deciding to stick together is different, as
long as they keep acting in their own best interests. But making a
deal to oust everyone else and split the last two VPs is a no-no.

>> I would object to most, if not all private communications under the
>> "collusion" rule. It's possible to gang up on someone, and it SHOULD
>> be possible (deal-making is an important part of this game), but it
>> shouldn't be EASY to do so,
>
>Why not? I thought VTES was a multiplayer game, not just a group of
>people who happen to be playing a series of two-player games at the
>same place and time. If it's easy for to people to gang up, then it's
>just as easy for the victim to make a counter-offer or gang up with
>someone else.

You can't make a counteroffer to something you never heard in the
first place. You can't enlist someone's help against something you
don't know is coming. You can try, but you will fail. This is why
individual extensive private discussions should not be involved -
because it IS a multiplayer game, and it is NOT Diplomacy.

>> >less fun because you can't show any cool cards you draw to anyone
>else
>> >(Hey, wow! I got an Archon Investigation to use against my Malkavian
>> >predator.)
>>
>> So you show it to everyone
>
>Actually, you can't do that either...

I'm perfectly aware of the current rule. Any "show cards" rule SHOULD
be in the form of "you must either show it to everyone or nobody."
Since you are in favor of showing cards, I assume you wish to show the
card to everyone. So...

>>and your Malkavian predator never bleeds
>> you for more than 3 at a time again - OR he bleeds you for 5 with
>> Ohanna, the disposable vampire. Wouldn't you rather keep it secret
>> and burn Ozmo's greasy butt when he comes with the Big Kaboom?
>
>Not if I only have 4 or 5 pool...
>All that does is screw both of us.

Your predator's job is first and foremost, to oust you. If he's a
sneak-bleed predator, he will be bleeding you. He has no other
options if he wants to act in his own best interests, ie. gain VPs and
WIN. Your AI ensures, for you, that he can't nail you for that 4 or 5
pool in one shot. If he has another vampire handy after the AI, you
will still die at 1 or 2 pool. If, however, you KEEP IT SECRET, then
he might spend some time setting up his defense for next turn,
assuming he will be able to bleed you out at any time, and then send
his last vampire to bleed for 6.

If you show the AI, you guarantee that he'll send the appropriate
number of vampires to ensure your oust. This would be a misplay - an
attempt to intimidate that failed. You can also SAY "i have an AI"
and produce the same effect.

I would personally rather lose one vampire and gain one VP as opposed
to sitting around hoping for you to, perhaps, completely lose your
mind and discard the AI. So if you have an AI, a Malk predator, and
you're at 5 pool, you're probably basically screwed - but you want to
make it as expensive as you can for your predator to take you out,
since most people will gladly sacrifice Ohanna (or even Ozmo!) for 1
VP and 6 more pool. Maybe he'll send Lucian instead.

>> You'll just have to work on your persuasion skills, eh? I have
>> difficulty coming up with a situation where I'd -want- to show an
>> erratic player (or even a non-erratic player) one of my cards.
>
>See the example above. I might be able to burn Ozmo with an Archon
>Investigation, but not particularly want to because it could severely
>weaken _both_ players.

This is a misplay, though. Your order of priority should be:

1) Oust my prey
2) Stay alive
3) Not waste time screwing up my predator

Assume Ozmo and Roland Bishop are behind you. You tell your predator
that you have an AI and will use it, and if he comes to bleed you,
you'll both be weakened severely and that would be a Bad Thing(tm).
He says "that's nice", and sends Roland to bleed for 5 (govern +
condition). You AI Roland, and he then sends Ozmo on a cardless bleed
to oust you since he KNOWS you're defenseless. He loses one 4-cap,
gains a VP and 6 pool. Bad call on your part.

Same situation, you don't tell him you have the AI. Roland makes a
better (read: more disposable) defender than Ozmo does, so he bleeds
with Ozmo for 6 (govern + condition). You AI Ozmo. Because you
didn't show a card or tell him, he has to decide whether you can stop
his one remaining vampire, and just decided to burn Ozmo for giggles
(and because it's freaking Ozmo). He may send Roland to bleed anyway,
but it's not an automatic choice anymore. (And, he needs another
bleed card.)

Almost the same situation, except it's just Ozmo behind you. You
absolutely want to burn Ozmo here, because that keeps you alive and
predator-free for another couple turns while he sets up again OR gets
ousted by his own predator, whichever. It shouldn't matter to you -
you can't gain that VP until after you oust your OWN prey.

Different situation: Ozmo and Roland behind you, except you have 15
pool now. This is the only time step #3 above comes into play - you
could tell your predator "If anyone bleeds me, I'm going to burn them
with AI". With any luck, he'll be scared and waste time defending
instead of bleeding you twice for 3 (which he ought to do).

[editorial: In all 4 of these, I'd keep my AI secret and burn a vamp.
Malk S&B isn't going to be any less sneaky-bleedy one turn from now,
and if I'm defenseless it's actually in my interest to get anything
BUT a Malk deck as my predator.]

>> Say
>> he's rushing cross-table and I say "I have a Skin of Steel. Don't
>> waste your time." If he believes me, that's good! If he doesn't,
>> well, I -do- have the Skin of Steel and his rush will go nowhere.
>> Sure, maybe I wanted to use it against my prey when he blocked one of
>> my bleeds, but that's life when you have an erratic player on the
>> table. Not all events are predictable.
>>
>> I think if I -really- wanted to save my SoS, I'd spend my time
>> explaining why rushing me cross-table didn't help him win the game.
>
>Thus extending a relatively simple task (i.e., showing the card), into
>a lengthy and potentially unneccessary discussion. I fail to see how
>slowing down a game that can take 15 mins or more between [your] turns
>is an improvement.

But showing the card doesn't fix his erratic play, and his erratic
play is what threatens my chances of winning. So maybe I show him my
SoS, and he goes elsewhere. My turn comes around, and I use my SoS
against my prey like I planned. Now his turn comes around and he DOES
IT AGAIN, because now he knows/thinks I don't have the SoS. I did
nothing to stop him from WANTING to Rush me - a misplay on my part.

And it doesn't have to be a lengthy discussion - usually just asking
the question "How exactly does this help you gain VPs?" brings them
back around to reality. If it doesn't, it's usually time to try and
make deals to gang up and oust that player before he unbalances the
table any more, and save the elaborate half-hour explanations for
later.

(It's entirely possible that showing the SoS would -guarantee- that he
Rushed me, especially if his whole purpose was just to burn through a
bunch of combat cards that he didn't need right then.)

OK. Politics involves bluffing. If you say "If you call that vote
against me, I'm going to Rush and kill that vampire. I have the Rush
in hand right now, so trust me, I CAN." If you can't show cards, he
HAS to decide whether or not you're bluffing. If you CAN show cards,
he just says "prove it", and your bluff mechanism no longer works.
Either you show the Rush, or you don't. If you don't show the Rush,
he assumes you're bluffing, since why would you NOT show him - you
don't want to Rush him, you want the vote not to be called. No good.

V:TES involves a lot of politics. Showing cards removes a significant
amount of the politics and reduces it to "if A, then B, then C."

The DCI Universal Penalty Guidelines prevent players from looking at

From:

122. Card Drawing--Looking at Extra Cards

Definition:

Players are considered to have looked at a card when the card is moved
any significant amount from the deck. This could include dropping cards
on the floor, turning a card over while shuffling their opponent's
deck, or revealing cards from their deck in the act of misplaying a
card. This penalty also applies when a player has looked at a card in
an opponent's deck or hand in the course of a game (such as turning
over an extra card while resolving a random discard effect).

A player is not considered to have looked at extra cards when he or she
places a card face down on the table (without looking at the card) in
an effort to count out cards he or she will draw.

---

player under the DCI Universal Tournament Rules: 1999-2000 Tournament
Season.

http://www.wizards.com/DCI/UTRules.asp

33. Card Elevation

Players must keep their cards above the level of the playing surface.
Revealing your hand to your opponent is not considered to be a
violation of the DCI Universal Tournament Rules.

---

Under these rules at least, it would seem looking at someone else's
hand, or your own library are prevented, while revealing your hand is
allowed.

For anyone who doesn't understand why collusion is bad, I suggest they
take up "Diplomacy" (the board game set in war-time Europe). There was
also a very good article in "The Duelist" by Richard Garfield on the
subject of king-making.

He invents a very simple game. Give three players each one counter. Now,
select one player to start at random. When it is a player's turn, they
choose someone to lose a counter. Thus, in this situation, the first
player cannot win. He can, however, king-make.

Collusion works on the same principle. Rather than people working to win
themselves (which is good, because it creates a challenging game), they
work to king-make their friend. This is bad. If I turn up to a random
tournament in America, no-one knowing who I am, I would hope I have as
much chance as everyone else. the fact that I can't turn up with friends
who (when they see they are going down) will just hand me all their
minions to use (effectively - I just tell him what I want done etc., or
something similar) shouldn't make a difference. It should rely on my deck
building skill, a little luck (shuffles), and my skill. It shouldn't turn
into a "Who can bring the most friends with them to unbalance the
tables" contest.

You're wrong -- you DON'T have a choice. If it is a well-known fact
that you CAN reveal your cards, and if revealing cards is commonly
used to prove that you're not bluffing, then it immediately becomes
the standard. Either you show a card and prove you're not bluffing,
or someone assumes you are bluffing and no deal gets made - often to
both people's disadvantage.

The previous Skin of Steel example is an excellent one. Player A is
being rushed cross-table by player B. A says "Don't do that, I'll
just prevent your damage and you'll hurt both of us." B says "I think
you're lying just to save your vampire. Prove it." A says "Nope. I
won't prove it, just trust me." Player B now Rushes, since if A
really had the prevent he'd show it in order to save the prevent card
- and it's in A's interest to say he has one whether or NOT he does.
A's "best course of action" is clearly defined to all by being able to
reveal cards, so B can now tell when player A is lying/bluffing simply
by when he deviates from that "best course". It becomes a vicious
circle, since player A -knows- that by saying "Don't do that" he'll
provoke a Rush, so he's more likely to show his cards, making it even
more of a standard.

politics, and the seamy side of the World of Darkness. If a
misunderstanding would be suboptimal, correct the misunderstanding,
don't just show the card.

The base rules specify (I think) how you should place your library, and
when you should draw cards. However, they do not specify how you should
position your hand. A literal interpretation of the rules could mean
that I could hold my hand so that it faces towards the other players,
but that they would not be able to 'look' at it (because of the rules
that specify what you can 'look' at). However, I interpreted 'look' to
be an active process, that is different to the passive process involved
in having a card placed directly in the centre of your field of vision.
It might sound a bit strange, but it does seem to be supported by the
DCI Universal tournament rules, that prevent 'looking' at other players
cards, but allow 'revealing' (i.e., the two processes are different).

You are confusing the dictionary definition of "hand" with the standard
meaning. You call it "missing something", but I suspect it is merely
"playing Devil's Advocate" now. It would be hard to imagine playing a
game as complex as V:TES without having some understanding of card
games to begin with.

For a more elaborate (more complete) explanation of "hand" and what
is expected of the player, see, for example, the "General Mechanics
of Card Games": http://www.pagat.com/mech.html

Excerpt from that page: "all players pick up their cards and hold
them in such a way that the faces can be seen by the holder of the
cards but not the other players."

Or see Scarne or Hoyle's rules of card games and note how penalties
for displaying cards are given, even though showing a card is never
"defined" as illegal.

Devil's Advocate or no, everything that needs to be said (and more)
in this thread has been said. Let's move on.
